# Plan: from a Clawd kit to a general motion-graphics video system

**Goal.** An agent can take a brief (product, message, brand, length) and produce any kind of motion-graphics launch
film in the style of the What Ships catalog (whatships.com): UI walkthroughs, kinetic type, feature montages, icon
choreography, abstract graphics, data reveals, illustrated character pieces. It does this with the same working method
as today: storyboard, then build, then look at its own contact sheets, then render.

**Out of scope.** Live-action footage, real people and photoreal 3D can't be generated by code. The system can
**composite** footage, screen recordings and product photos that you supply (Phase 3). Measured over all 2,221 films
(Phase 0): 41.7% can be made entirely in code, 16.2% can with supplied assets, and 41.3% need a camera. Even so, 63% of
the camera-led films carry designed overlays (titles, captions, logos, UI) that this engine can make.

**Decisions** (defaults, change them here if you disagree):
- Extend this engine rather than move to Remotion. We keep the small, agent-friendly core (frames are pure functions of
  `t`, headless Chrome, contact-sheet review) and the MIT licence.
- Include compositing of supplied footage and recordings (Phase 3).

---

## Phase 0: reference catalog *(done)*

Sections 0.1–0.3 cover **the whole catalog**; 0.4 and 0.5 measure the films themselves for a sample. Scripts are in `scripts/` and outputs in `refs/whatships/`.

**0.1 Index:** `whatships_index.mjs`.
- The slug set is the union of `search-index.json` and `sitemap.xml`, which list the same 2,221 videos.
- Every entry is parsed: title, product, company, category, date, duration, author, X link, tags and description.
- The source video's resolution is read from the URL embedded in each page, without downloading anything. It's known
  for 2,213 films; the 8 others have no video URL.
- It also indexes the 78 tools and 7 studios. `--posters` saves all 2,221 poster frames.
- The run fails on any missing or unparseable entry.
- Output: `catalog.json` and `catalog.md`.
- Snapshot (2026-09-26): AI 897 · Developer tools 436 · Other 327 · Design 207 · Consumer 135 · Productivity 92 ·
  Hardware 80 · Motion 47. Median length 53 s. 91% landscape, 5% square, 3.5% vertical.

**0.2 Visual tags:**
- `whatships_grids.mjs` packs every poster into 139 numbered 4×4 grids.
- Ten vision subagents tagged every cell with a fixed taxonomy: medium, overlays, background, text level and a note.
- `whatships_tags.mjs` validates coverage (every slug tagged exactly once, all values from the taxonomy) and writes
  `visual.json` and `visual.md`.
- "Can code make it?" is **derived by one rule** from the tags, so it's consistent across taggers. Each tagger's own
  call is kept as `feasible_agent`.
- A spot-check of a full grid against the posters found all 16 tags correct.

**0.3 Families and recipes:**
- `whatships_genres.mjs` sorts every film into one of 11 visual families (plus blank). It picks 16 representatives
  per family, spread across categories, and writes `genres.json` and `genres.md` (with X citations) and a grid per
  family.
- Recipes for each family are in `docs/genres/`: stats, what it looks like (74 cited films), beats, motion
  vocabulary, engine needs and pitfalls.

**Findings that change the plan** (0.4 and 0.5 add motion and design defaults: see
`docs/motion_design_spec.md`):
- **Text is the norm:** 75.7% of films show text, and 10.9% are dominated by it. Phase 4 replaces "no text" with
  typography rules.
- **Light backgrounds are as common as dark** (25.5% vs 23.7%). In UI films it's 50% light and 28% dark. Themes need
  light and dark tokens, and the default must not be dark.
- **Square and vertical exist** (5% and 3.5%). The engine needs a configurable canvas size, not a fixed 1920×1080
  (Phase 2).
- **Cursors appear in 22–24% of UI films,** so the cursor is a first-class component.
- **Code-makeable films are short:** a median of 35–49 s by family, mostly 20–75 s.
- **UI and type together are 43.5% of the catalog** (UI walkthrough 17.2%, type-led 14.3%, screen demo 12.0%). These
  come first in Phase 2.

**0.4 Pacing and structure (213 films):**
- `whatships_pacing.mjs` downloads about 20 films per family, measures them, and deletes them: hard cuts, shot lengths,
  still time and audio.
- It also makes a labelled 1-frame-per-second sheet of each film. Ten vision subagents annotated every film's beats
  (kind, start, end), first text, first product appearance, end card, transitions, camera and pace.
- `whatships_pacing_summary.mjs` refuses to run if any film is missing its annotation, and writes `pacing.md`.
- Findings:
  - One beat about every 5 s.
  - UI, screen and graphic films show the product at 0 s.
  - End cards appear in 65–88% of designed films and last 3.3–4.6 s.
  - Designed films run 31–49 s.
- 3 films couldn't be fetched because their source links are dead.

**0.5 Craft of the top tier (36 films):**
- `top_tier.json` is films by the listed studios, the Motion category, and design-led product teams.
- `whatships_craft.py` measures every move from 24 fps frame differences: length, easing shape, stagger peaks and
  holds. It also measures tempo and beat alignment, and the palette and contrast of full-resolution stills.
- Six vision subagents read every frame of 198 key moves (settle time, overshoot, stagger, style) and 141 stills (type
  sizes, weights, alignment, margins, radius, shadow, background).
- `whatships_craft_summary.py` writes `craft.md`. The results are turned into defaults in
  **`docs/motion_design_spec.md`**.
- Headlines:
  - **Overshoot almost never appears** (97% of moves have none).
  - Moves take about 0.58 s, mostly with a balanced ease-in-out; cards are fast ease-out, over about 9 frames.
  - The stagger between items is 4 frames. Holds between moves are about 1.25 s.
  - Cuts land on the beat no more often than chance.
  - Frames use one sans family at regular weight, with a headline cap height of about 44 px at 1080p.
  - There's one accent colour and low saturation, and 54% of stills are light.
  - Margins are about 13% of the width, corner radius about 28 px, and most frames have no shadow.

The videos were only analysed: each was deleted right after measurement, and nothing from them is used in anything
we make.

Policy: the site allows crawling (`robots.txt` Allow /) and asks for citation with the original X link. We study
patterns only and never copy brands, footage or assets.

---

## Phase 1: generalise the engine *(done, see 1.7 for the results)*

Keep the core rule: **every frame is a pure function of `t`.** Add a second drawing surface, the DOM (HTML, CSS and
SVG), because launch films are mostly polished UI and typography, which the browser renders natively (real fonts,
blur, shadows, glass, gradients, 2.5D transforms).

### 1.1 Scene manifest and loader
Right now `studio.html` hard-codes one character and one scene, and `clawd.js` and `jolly.js` clash on globals (`EMO`,
`feel`, `VIEWS`, …).
- `src/scenes/index.js` defines `LIBS` (named groups of script files) and `SCENES`. Each scene has `file`, `libs` and
  `project` (overrides for `PROJECT`: duration, style, bpm, fonts, canvasBg).
- `studio.html?scene=<name>` loads exactly that scene's libs and file, in order and synchronously.
  `render.mjs --scene=<name>` passes it through. The default comes from `PROJECT.scene` in config.js.
- Result: Clawd, Jolly and the new motion-graphics scenes all run from one studio, each loading only what it needs.

### 1.2 DOM layer: `src/dom.js`
Immediate-mode API with a retained DOM underneath. It works like p5: each frame, the shot *declares* everything on
screen; the engine reuses the elements, applies the new properties, and removes whatever wasn't declared.
- Stage: `#stage`, 1920×1080. Paint order is call order.
- Calls: `D.div(key?, props?, kids?)`, `D.text(key?, str, props?)`, `D.img(key?, src, props?)`,
  `D.svg(key?, props?, kids?)` plus SVG children (`D.path`, `D.circle`, `D.rect`, `D.g`, …),
  `D.el(tag, key?, props?, kids?)`, `D.group`, `D.cam(cx, cy, zoom, rot, kids)` and `D.canvas()`.
- Props: `x, y, w, h`, anchor `ax, ay` (0..1), `scale / sx / sy`, `rot` (degrees), `rx, ry` (2.5D tilt) with
  `persp`, `opacity`, `blur`, `z`, `cls`, `style` (any CSS; numbers become px where they're lengths), `attrs`,
  `html`/`text`, and `pos: 'abs' | 'flow'` (stage children default to absolute, nested children to normal flow, so
  flexbox UI layouts just work).
- Purity guarantees:
  1. Every managed style and attribute that isn't declared this frame is removed.
  2. Elements not declared this frame are removed.
  3. CSS animations and transitions are disabled under `#stage`, and SVG SMIL is paused. Motion comes only from `t`.
  4. Keys are optional (the default key is tag plus call index within the parent). Explicit keys only save work,
     for example avoiding image re-decodes; correctness doesn't depend on them.
- Readiness: a frame isn't captured until every image has decoded and every font is loaded. Fonts listed in
  `PROJECT.fonts` are preloaded at startup.
- Camera: `D.cam` does the same maths as `camBegin` and sets `LAST_CAM`, so `--crop-at` works on DOM scenes too.

### 1.3 Layers: mixing p5 and DOM
- `D.canvas()` places the p5 painting (`#out`) at that point in the paint order. For example: DOM background, then
  p5 particles, then a DOM UI card.
- `PROJECT.canvasBg: null` makes the p5 canvas transparent (no paper, no grain) so layers underneath show through.
- A frame that declares DOM but no `D.canvas()` hides the canvas. Pure p5 scenes are unchanged.

### 1.4 Renderer: one capture path for both surfaces
- `window.seek(t)` in the page renders the frame at `t` and waits until it's ready. Pure-canvas frames are still read
  straight from the canvas (fast, and byte-identical to today). Frames with DOM are captured with a Chrome screenshot
  of the stage at a fixed 1920×1080 viewport and scale factor 1.
- Contact sheets, strips, crops (`--crop`, `--crop-at`), stills, PNG loops, `--frames` (parallel, resumable) and
  `--clip` all go through that one capture function. Sheets are assembled on a separate composer page.

### 1.5 Studio
The stage scales to fit the preview, with a scrub bar, play/pause (space bar) and a scene picker. `?render` shows the
bare stage for capture.

### 1.6 Demo scene: `mg_demo`
An 11-second launch film for a fictional product. It exercises every Phase 1 feature: kinetic type from a dark open,
a zoom-through transition, a macOS-style app window with 2.5D tilt, a cursor with clicks, typing, a result card
springing in, a toast, p5 glow particles as a layer between DOM layers, a logo end card and a fade out.

### 1.7 Verification (results)
- **No regression:** Muse scene stills at 5 times are **byte-identical** before and after (the MD5s match the
  baselines in `out/check/baseline`). The painted Clawd demo renders through `?scene=clawd`.
- **Determinism:**
  - Canvas frames are byte-identical.
  - `mg_demo` stills rendered in forward, reverse and mixed order were byte-identical, except one frame that differed
    by at most **1/255 in one channel** (PSNR 78 dB). A repeat run matched the forward run exactly, and software
    rasterisation shows the same occasional noise. So it's Chrome raster noise, not scene state.
  - Result: DOM frames are identical up to invisible ±1 raster noise.
- **Coverage:** on `mg_demo`, all of these work: sheets, strips, `--crop-at` following a world point through `D.cam`,
  stills, and `--frames` with 4 workers (264 frames in 16 s, about 53 ms/frame) followed by `--encode` (MP4, 11.0 s,
  1920×1080). Frames now go to `out/frames/<scene>` so scenes never mix.
- **Bugs found and fixed while verifying:**
  - Reused elements lost their gradients: setting a CSS shorthand then removing a stale longhand wiped it. `D` now
    rewrites a changed element's whole style declaration in order.
  - A logo pop overlapped the fading headline (two reads at once), so it was retimed.
- **Docs:** a DOM-layer section in `ANIMATION_GUIDE.md`, scene manifest steps, and the README.

## Phase 2 status: done
- **Built:**
  - Configurable canvas (`PROJECT.size`).
  - Theme tokens: light and dark, with brand overrides.
  - Measured motion presets with no overshoot by default.
  - `lib/type`, `lib/ui`, `lib/cursor`, `lib/shapes`, `lib/fx` (gradient, glow, grain, vignette, closed-form particles
    with ring, grid and text targets), `lib/camera` (keyframed shots, parallax, depth of field), `lib/transitions`
    (dip, wipe, iris, grid covers; whip and zoom moves; layout morph) and `lib/brand` (mark, lock-up, end card,
    partner lock-up, safe area).
  - A real cross-dissolve between shots (`xfade`).
  - Namespaced characters (`Clawd`, `Jolly`) with one interface, so two can share a scene (`duo`).
  - Model sheets for every library (`?scene=kit&loop=kit_*`, stills in `docs/kit/`).
- **Demos:**
  - `launch_demo`: a 24 s UI walkthrough in landscape, square, vertical and dark.
  - `relay_demo`: a 20.5 s brand and type film.
- **Verified:**
  - MP4s for `launch_demo` (landscape and vertical) and `relay_demo`.
  - The Muse and Clawd scenes are byte-identical before and after all Phase 2 changes, including namespacing.
  - `relay_demo` frames mixing particles and DOM are byte-identical across render orders.
- **Fixed in review:**
  - Word gaps.
  - A comment that swallowed the typing props.
  - Headline overflow on the square canvas.
  - A needless camera pull-back.
  - Muddy light gradients and vignettes.
  - Overlapping word swaps, now one read at a time.
  - Word holds that were shorter than the reading rule.
- **Deferred:**
  - Optional per the plan: a WebGL layer for stylised 3D.
  - Nice to have: pixel-art and line-art character styles, a sphere sampler, glitch and light-streak effects, an
    auto-fit text box, and a word-to-icon morph.
  - None of these block Phase 3.

## Phase 3 status: done
- **Built:**
  - A frame-exact video layer (`D.video`): each frame seeks to its media time and capture waits for it.
  - `lib/media`: clip timing with offset, rate, loop and speed ramps, and the inverse `filmTime` for syncing sounds;
    colour treatments, duotone, Ken Burns and scrims; phone, tablet, laptop and browser device frames; WebVTT and SRT
    captions with word highlighting; lower thirds.
  - `lib/audio` (`Sound`): music bed, sound-effect cues, clips, cursor clicks and typing taps, declared at load. The
    mix in `render.mjs` handles `--clip` and `--encode`: trim, delay, level, mix, loudnorm to −15 LUFS and −1.5 dBTP.
  - A generated sound-effect library (`scripts/make_sfx.mjs`, from expressions only).
  - Project folders (`projects/<name>/`: brief, `project.js`, assets, scene) with local brand fonts, and a brief
    template.
- **Verified:**
  - `check_video_frames.mjs`: 40 of 40 frames exact, at 1× and at 0.5× with an offset, in shuffled order.
  - `footage_demo` (21 s): mixed sound at −14.7 LUFS, with all 17 cues found in the mix within 30 ms of plan,
    including clicks re-timed through a speed ramp.
  - Muse, Clawd and Relay frames are byte-identical after all Phase 3 changes.
- **Fixed in review:**
  - The frame-counter test first failed because video luma is limited range. Measured: shown = (Y − 16) · 255/219.
    The test now encodes levels inside the range.
  - Noise baked into stand-in footage made a 375 MB file. The grain now comes from `FX.grain`.
  - `Audio` would have shadowed the browser's `Audio`, so it's renamed `Sound`.
  - The typing sound times duplicated the typing jitter. Both now use `Type.charTimes`.
  - The lower third and the captions shared a line.
- **Not yet:**
  - Text behind a person needs a supplied alpha matte (WebM with alpha as a top layer). There's no automatic
    segmentation.
  - Captions are pasted into `project.js`, because `studio.html` opened from disk can't fetch files.
  - No voice-over generation: supply the file.

## Phase 2 priorities (from Phase 0)
1. Configurable canvas: 16:9, 1:1 and 9:16, with safe areas.
2. Theme tokens: light and dark as equals.
3. `lib/type` and `lib/ui` with the cursor (together they cover 43.5% of the catalog).
4. `lib/shapes` and `lib/brand` (end cards are used by every family).
5. `lib/fx` (particles, gradients, glow).
6. Optionally, a WebGL layer for stylised 3D.

---

## Phase 2: motion-graphics library (`src/lib/`)
Everything here is a pure function of `t` built on `seg / ease / kf / spring`, and each part has a model sheet
(`?loop=`) so the agent can see it.
- **Type:** reveals per word and per letter (rise, blur, mask, stagger), counters and tickers, highlight and
  underline sweeps, text morphing into a logo, lower thirds, auto-fit to a box.
- **UI kit:** window frames (macOS, browser, phone, tablet), cursor (move along an arc, click ripple, drag), typing
  with a caret, chat bubbles, command palette, cards, toasts, menus, tables, charts (bar, line, number), skeleton
  loaders, notification stacks.
- **Camera:** 2.5D push, tilt and orbit of UI planes, depth-of-field blur, rack focus, zoom-through-screen, parallax
  layers.
- **Transitions:** mask wipes (shape or text), zoom-through, blur-whip, match cut, shared-element move, grid split,
  iris (existing).
- **Looks:** gradient meshes, grain, grids and dot fields, glow and bloom, glass, noise backgrounds, light and dark
  presets.
- **Motion presets:** named springs (snappy UI, soft, bouncy) and staggers.
- Characters (Clawd, Jolly, humans) become namespaced libs with one shared interface, so several can share a scene.

## Phase 3: inputs
- `brief.md`: product, the single message, audience, length, genre, call to action.
- `brand/`: logo SVG, colours and fonts, turned into theme tokens that every lib component reads.
- `assets/`: screenshots, product photos, and **screen recordings and footage** as video layers seeked to `t`
  (frame-exact: seek, wait for `seeked`, then capture), with device frames and masks.
- Audio: music is muxed and beat-synced (already exists). Add sound effects (whoosh, click, pop) placed at event
  times and mixed in the encode step.

## Phase 4: rewrite the guide
- Keep the general rules: timing and reads, one focal point, transitions at every seam, nothing still, the review
  loop.
- Replace "no text" with typography rules (hierarchy, words on screen for long enough to read, safe areas).
- Add a section per genre (links to `docs/genres/`), and keep the character-cartoon rules as one of the genres.
- Add brief-to-storyboard templates for each genre.

## Phase 5: evaluate
For each genre, pick 2–3 catalog references and make a comparable film for a fictional product. Compare contact
sheets side by side against the references (poster frames and pacing notes) and iterate on the library and guide.
Track failures as guide rules.
